title: DoubleTree Fire: Judge Orders Evidence Preserved as Chief Recounts the Night of the Blaze

content:
A judge has granted three court orders in the lawsuit against the owner of Laredo’s DoubleTree hotel, including an order requiring both sides to preserve evidence from the Oct. 7 fire — as the city’s fire chief gave his fullest public account yet of the night the 14-story hotel burned.

Judge Beckie Palomo ordered the preservation of relevant records, photos and video, according to a Nov. 16 report. The lawsuit was filed against the hotel’s owner; the plaintiffs were not named in the reporting available to Webb Watch 956.

Speaking to the Laredo Gateway Rotary Club, Fire Chief Guillermo Heard described the Oct. 7 blaze as among the biggest the department has fought in roughly three decades. The 911 call came at about 12:52 a.m., with fire burning on the hotel’s fifth floor.

Roughly 80 firefighters responded, and more than 120 people were inside the building, most of them National Guard members. Four people were taken to the hospital for smoke inhalation and four more drove themselves for care. All eight were released. “Nobody died. Nobody got seriously hurt,” Heard said.

Crews kept re-entering to evacuate guests and check rooms until they noticed the sixth floor felt “spongy” underfoot and spotted exposed structural steel. With no one left inside, Heard said, the call was made to withdraw, since the department ranks saving lives above saving property. Drones later documented the structural damage.

The site remains active. A structural engineering company retained by the property’s owner is shoring up the building, a collapse zone has been set up and crews remain on fire watch. Investigators from the Laredo Fire Department, the Texas State Fire Marshal’s Office and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives cannot fully enter until stabilization is finished. The cause of the fire has still not been determined.

Asked about sprinklers, Heard said the hotel met the building code in force when it was built and renovated and was equipped with sprinklers, but he would not elaborate while the investigation continues. He also noted that hotel alarms normally warn only the floor involved and the floors directly above and below it.

Heard also addressed department staffing: authorized strength is 469 firefighters, and the department has just over 420. He pointed to the pandemic and to the fire department’s pension plan, which operates apart from the city’s, as the causes, and said he has moved administrative employees into line jobs. Two more fire stations are planned, near the Buena Vista station and in the Unitec area, with construction expected to last 12 to 18 months once it starts. Fire trucks that cost about half a million dollars before the pandemic now cost about $1 million, he said.

On firefighter wellness, Heard said the department employs a psychologist, runs a peer support team and has opened a wellness center in a former fire station on Del Mar Boulevard. He said a firefighter died by suicide in August, which affected colleagues, and called firefighter mental health “one of the things that we’re really concerned about.”

Sources: Apex News Latam, Nov. 16, 2026; Local National, Nov. 18, 2026; OpenTexas, DoubleTree Hotel emergency.
